A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
Experimental drug invika halts progression of refractory tumors by selectively stimulating tumor-fighting T cells.
Early results of the first clinical trial to evaluate the drug invikafusp alfa (invika) in humans indicate that the pioneering treatment may be capable of managing cancers that have rebuffed most other interventions, including standard immunotherapy. A study led by researchers at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Mass General Brigham and Memorial Sloan Kettering found that, at optimal doses, invika was well tolerated and, in patients whose solid tumors had resisted standard immunotherapy, halted disease progression in most and shrank tumors in some.
“Patients whose tumors are advanced — particularly tumors that don’t respond well to immunotherapy — often have their backs against a wall. Few options remain once you reach that point, but these results highlight a more precise means of stimulating anti-tumor immunity that could provide another solution,” said co-corresponding author James Gulley, M.D., Ph.D., clinical director at the Center for Cancer Research (CCR), part of NIH’s National Cancer Institute (NCI).
While immunotherapies have already transformed treatment for several cancers, many patients benefit from them for only a short time, or not at all. Tumors frequently adapt to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies, such as pembrolizumab, limiting long-term benefits. Other strategies aim to rally T cells, the frontline soldiers of adaptive immunity, but usually do so indiscriminately, commonly leading to severe side effects.
Scientists designed the protein invika to engage a small subset of T cells, two groups of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes specifically. By activating only this narrow population rather than T cells broadly, invika is designed to drive anti-tumor activity while avoiding the severe side effects that less selective approaches can cause. Preclinical studies also conducted at CCR indicate that the drug hits its intended marks and stimulates anti-tumor activity in animal models. This new study describes the next step for invika, detailing the results of phase 1 and initial phase 2 experiments in humans.
The researchers leading the trial recruited patients with a wide variety of cancers, the majority of which had not responded well to ICB. In phase 1, they treated study participants with varying dosages of invika every two weeks to evaluate the drug’s safety and determine the optimal dose. While several participants experienced flu-like side effects, these were expected and generally manageable with additional medication and supportive care. After identifying the lowest dose at which desired effects peaked, the researchers advanced to phase 2, treating participants at this optimal dose.
Of the 27 participants treated with the optimal dose across both phases, disease did not progress in 16 (59.3%) of them. Four (14.8%) participants experienced greater than 30% decreases in the size of targeted tumors, two of whom had metastatic colorectal cancer with tumors of a notoriously treatment-resistant type and were receiving invika as their seventh-line therapy. Another responsive participant had stage 4 non-small cell lung cancer, again with tumors that had repelled multiple therapies including ICB. In participants receiving non-optimal levels, invika did not appear to have significant benefit.
In these patients, the study authors found that the drug fostered growth in the target T-cell populations without affecting any other T cells. They linked the four instances of tumor reduction to the largest shifts in target populations, though, as the authors expected at this early stage, immune activity alone did not always produce a measurable clinical response.
“These results are early, and although signs of immune activity don't always translate into benefit to patients at this stage, it is new and exciting to see activity in patients whose cancers had stopped responding to immunotherapy — a group of people with very few options left,” said co-first author Nicholas Tschernia, M.D., a physician-scientist early investigator in the CCR at NCI. “These findings give us a reason to keep studying this new type of immunotherapy, particularly by combining it with other cancer treatments to continue to seek improved results.”
The treatment sponsor, Marengo Therapeutics, previously announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted a Fast Track designation to invika to accelerate its evaluation as a treatment for antigen-rich, metastatic colorectal cancer. More recently, FDA has granted the same designation to invika for similar solid tumors, regardless of tissue type, following prior therapy including checkpoint inhibitors.
The ongoing clinical trial is still seeking study participants. Patients interested in enrolling in this study may contact NCI’s toll-free number 1-800-4-Cancer (1-800-422-6237) (TTY: 1-800-332-8615) or email [email protected]. More information can also be found at https://www.trials.cancer.gov.
About the National Cancer Institute (NCI): NCI leads the National Cancer Program and NIH’s efforts to dramatically reduce the prevalence of cancer and improve the lives of cancer patients and their families, through research into prevention and cancer biology, the development of new interventions, and the training and mentoring of new researchers. NCI’s intramural research program at the Center for Cancer Research (CCR) conducts innovative, transdisciplinary basic, translational, and clinical studies, including research at the NIH Clinical Center — the world’s largest research hospital. Learn more about the intramural research done in NCI’s CCR. For more information about cancer, please visit the NCI website at www.cancer.gov or call NCI’s contact center, the Cancer Information Service, at 1-800-4-CANCER (1-800-422-6237).
About the National Institutes of Health (NIH): NIH, the nation's medical research agency, includes 27 Institutes and Centers and is a component of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. NIH is the primary federal agency conducting and supporting basic, clinical, and translational medical research, and is investigating the causes, treatments, and cures for both common and rare diseases. For more information about NIH and its programs, visit www.nih.gov.

Surveying the genetic battlefield to uncover the rules of rapid evolution
The Malik Lab thrives on competition. But for HHMI investigator Harmit Malik and his team at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, it's the genomes—not the people—that are in conflict. The lab studies rapid evolution—the genetic changes that happen in a species over a few generations rather than thousands of years. These fast changes are often fueled by genetic conflicts—competitions between different entities trying to maximize their success at the expense of another.
By uncovering the evolutionary rules that guide these conflicts, Malik and his team are revealing insights that could help in the development of better disease treatments.
"Not only do these rules help us to look back in evolution and understand how these arms races played out, but these rules also let us look forward and come up with new strategies," Malik says.
Discovering a viral thermometer
One of the competitions the lab studies is the conflict between mosquito-borne alphaviruses like Sindbis and chikungunya and their hosts. These viruses are successful at infecting both insects and humans despite the different body temperatures and immune systems of these hosts.
The team, including postdoc Tamanash Bhattacharya, recently uncovered a carefully calibrated system that helps enable this versatility. A special stop codon in the virus's genome, which signals the cell to halt protein production, enables a "kinetic Goldilocks": It allows the virus to produce just enough of a critical polyprotein to survive, but not too much to slow down other processes that would lead to a decline in the virus's fitness.
In humans, where body temperatures are hotter and replication happens quickly, the virus relies on this codon, called the opal codon, to enable this production balancing act. In mosquitoes, where temperatures are colder and replication slows down, this balancing act isn't necessary, and the virus does not need to rely on this special stop codon.
Hiding from the immune system
These insights led the team to another question: Why is the opal codon still found in alphaviruses that only infect mosquitoes, even though its special properties aren't needed?
In new research, also led by Bhattacharya, the team found that in both humans and insects, the opal codon enables the virus to create a compartment where it can replicate without being seen by the host's immune system. If the opal codon is lost, viral replication becomes more visible and more susceptible to host immunity.
"This is one of the simplest and most elegant ways to hide yourself from immunity, and the fact that it is universally conserved in alphaviruses just reinforces how important it is," Malik says.
Now, the team is working to understand other built-in strategies these viruses use to thrive in different hosts, including the ability to quickly ramp up fitness in one host at the expense of the other.
"Learning the rules by which they do this gives us insight into the sheer adaptive possibilities that these genomes can experience," Malik says. "That's important because any attempts to make new antivirals will have to take this into account."
Evolution of essential genes
It might seem counterintuitive, but essential genes that organisms need to survive, grow and reproduce are often among the fastest evolving. The Malik Lab is uncovering these changes and why they occur.
New research, published in Science Advances and led by graduate student Jeremy Hollis, examines HJURP, a chaperon protein that marks the centromere, the site where chromosomes are pulled apart during cell division.
Despite its importance, scientists couldn't find HJURP in many animals. The Malik Lab used remote homology detection, AlphaFold-based structural modeling and functional genetic techniques to show that most animals do have HJURP. Because the protein evolves so rapidly, possibly to keep pace with other fast-changing centromere components, conventional tools couldn't detect it.
Separate research, also published in Science Advances led by former postdoc Ching-Ho Chang, investigated Mst77F, a protamine that packages DNA in fruit fly sperm. Protamines, which are essential for male fertility, are among the fastest-evolving genes in animals, and scientists couldn't figure out why. The Malik Lab found that Mst77F is rapidly evolving to suppress a form of genetic cheating that kills X-bearing sperm and skews broods toward sons.
Publication details

candidato.titulo: A 1,000-mile cloud on Mars may reveal physics never seen in nature
candidato.resumo: A new model suggests Mars may host ice-forming physics never directly observed before.

texto_fonte:
Every morning during the Martian spring and summer, a thin and extremely long cloud emerges, only to disappear again. The wispy formation appears near the volcano Arsia Mons and gradually elongates until it reaches over 1,000 miles—about the distance from New York to Kansas City as the crow flies—before dissipating. This cycle then repeats for several months.
Since it was first recorded by a probe in 2018, scientists have been unable to find a plausible explanation for the existence of this cloud, often referred to as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC). Until now. Recently, researchers successfully modeled the cloud’s formation for the first time, their results suggesting that it may be driven by a physical process that has never been directly observed in any planet’s atmosphere.
“We found that we needed to include some exotic physics… physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before,” Jorge Hernández-Bernal, a planetary scientist at Paris’ Sorbonne Université and lead author of the study, said in a press release. “Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped.”

O que são os TOPS dos chips de IA?
Por Raphael Giannotti • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
Se você acompanhou os últimos lançamentos de hardware, certamente reparou na presença insistente de uma sigla (nova para muitos) nas fichas técnicas: TOPS. Promovida por gigantes como Intel, AMD, Qualcomm e Nvidia, essa métrica se tornou a principal bandeira do marketing para definir o quão inteligente ou preparado para a era da IA um determinado dispositivo é.
Na prática, a sigla significa Trillions of Operations Per Second (Trilhões de Operações Por Segundo) e serve como uma medida teórica do desempenho bruto de um processador em tarefas de aprendizado de máquina. No entanto, por trás desse número, existe uma série de aspectos técnicos sobre como esse cálculo é feito, o papel da precisão dos dados e a real diferença entre processadores domésticos e chips voltados para servidores.
O que essa métrica realmente mede?
Para entender o conceito, vale imaginar os TOPS como a taxa de rotações por segundo de um motor, mas voltada para o processamento de redes neurais. Um pico de 40 TOPS indica que aquele circuito integrado é capaz de realizar matematicamente até 40 trilhões de operações numéricas simples por segundo na teoria, geralmente medindo cálculos de multiplicação e acúmulo.
No entanto, essa contagem depende diretamente do nível de precisão matemática utilizado pelo chip, expresso em formatos como INT8 (números inteiros de 8 bits), INT4 ou ponto flutuante (FP16). Como operações de menor precisão exigem menos energia e banda de memória para serem calculadas, a maioria das fabricantes divulga suas taxas de TOPS baseando-se no padrão INT8, que é o mais comum em tarefas de inferência de IA sem perda perceptível de qualidade.
O desempenho com NPU, CPU e iGPU
Nos PCs e notebooks de última geração, a métrica de TOPS costuma ser subdividida em três partes internas de um chip. O grande destaque dessa nova safra é a NPU (Neural Processing Unit), um bloco de silício projetado especificamente para executar tarefas de IA em segundo plano com consumo de energia extremamente baixo.
Enquanto a NPU de um notebook moderno entrega entre 40 e 50 TOPS para manter recursos como enquadramento automático de câmera, isolamento de ruído por voz ou recursos do Copilot+, a iGPU (gráfico integrado) e a CPU do processador também contribuem com suas próprias cotas de processamento. A soma desses três componentes gera o chamado "TOPS da plataforma", embora uma aplicação raramente consiga utilizar todos esses núcleos diferentes simultaneamente.
Placas de vídeo são os monstros de inferência em IA
Apesar do forte marketing em cima das NPUs integradas para notebooks, quando o assunto é desempenho bruto dentro do ecossistema doméstico, as placas de vídeo dedicadas (ou GPUs dedicadas de notebooks) continuam reinando absolutas. Modelos de entrada e intermediários de arquiteturas recentes superam facilmente a casa das centenas de TOPS, enquanto placas topo de linha alcançam patamares superiores a 1.000 TOPS (ou 1 Petaflop).
Essa disparidade brutal acontece porque as GPUs dedicadas possuem milhares de núcleos paralelos e barramentos de memória VRAM muito mais rápidos, essenciais para rodar modelos de linguagem locais (LLMs) pesados ou gerar imagens via inteligência artificial generativa em poucos segundos. A contrapartida dessa potência extrema é o consumo elevado, justificando a coexistência da NPU para tarefas leves do cotidiano e da GPU dedicada para cargas de trabalho brutas.
Aceleradores para data centers e supercomputadores
Quando saímos do ambiente doméstico e entramos nos data centers que treinam e hospedam os grandes modelos de IA do mercado, a métrica de TOPS atinge proporções totalmente diferentes. Processadores corporativos e aceleradores dedicados para servidores, como as famílias NVIDIA RTX Pro ou AMD Instinct, são projetados para lidar com petabytes de dados e distribuir cálculos pesados em milhares de nós interconectados.
Diferente do mercado de consumo, onde o foco está na inferência rápida e eficiente com precisão INT8, os chips de data center precisam entregar milhares de TOPS em precisões flutuantes complexas, como FP16, BF16 e FP8, que garantem a exatidão matemática necessária durante o treinamento de novos modelos. Nesses ambientes, a métrica de TOPS vem sempre acompanhada de exigências pesadas em largura de banda de memória (possíveis com as memórias HBM) e sistemas avançados de refrigeração líquida.
TOPS teóricos vs. desempenho real no dia a dia
Por fim, é crucial entender que uma taxa alta de TOPS no papel não garante automaticamente uma experiência mais rápida na rotina do usuário. O desempenho real de qualquer aplicação de inteligência artificial depende de uma cadeia complexa que envolve a otimização do software para aquela arquitetura, o suporte dos drivers e, principalmente, a largura de banda da memória RAM do sistema.
Se um processador possui uma NPU poderosa que entrega 50 TOPS, mas o modelo de linguagem que o usuário tenta rodar não cabe na memória RAM disponível ou enfrenta gargalos de transferência de dados, o chip passará mais tempo esperando a entrega de informações do que efetivamente processando. Portanto, ao avaliar um novo PC para IA, os TOPS devem ser vistos como um teto teórico de capacidade e não como a única garantia de velocidade.

candidato.titulo: Ice sheet expansion may have started 2,000 years ago, but we canceled that
candidato.resumo: The tiny remains of the Laurentide Ice Sheet began getting somewhat less tiny.

texto_fonte:
Barnes Ice Cap sits on the central plateau of Baffin Island, in the Canadian Arctic. It is the last surviving fragment of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, which at its peak buried most of Canada under two miles of ice and locked away around 80 meters of sea level. That remnant has now yielded direct physical evidence that ice sheets might have reversed their retreat and started to grow again thousands of years ago.
In a recent Science study, researchers show that the Laurentide reached its smallest size about 3,600 years ago, then started re-expanding roughly 2,000 years ago, which the team interprets as the opening move of the next glaciation. Apparently, this brand-new ice age was on its way until about 1960, when human-caused climate warming reversed it.
Frozen to the bed
“Barnes is the last remaining piece of one of the domes of the Laurentide Ice Sheet,” says Nicolás Young, a geologist at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory and lead author of the study. As that enormous dome thinned through the Holocene, its margin withdrew up onto Baffin Island, and what’s left today is the deflated core of something that was once two miles thick. The reason Barnes can testify about its own history, Young explains, comes down to the temperature at its base.
Most glaciers are warm-based, meaning meltwater at the bed lets them slide, and sliding ice grinds up everything beneath it, erasing the record. Barnes is cold-based, and thus frozen directly onto the bedrock beneath it, which prevents it from sliding.
“If there is an ice event where you live and you have to go and scrape off your windshield, that ice that’s plastered to the windshield of your car, that’s a good example of how cold-based ice operates. It’s sort of just stuck to what it’s on,” Young says.
This stuck ice preserves what’s beneath instead of eroding it. As the Laurentide retreated across the plateau, tundra plants colonized the newly bare ground. When the ice came back later, it simply smothered them in place and held them there, intact, for two millennia. To pinpoint the exact moment of this turnaround, Young’s team used two independent dating methods.

texto_fonte:
Whether voters are alive or dead is of vital interest to democracies. Yet unscrupulous political operators have long voted on behalf of the dead or absent and otherwise committed electoral frauds exploiting the weaknesses of paper identification systems. So some 50 countries now use biometric technologies, such as fingerprint readers or facial recognition technology, at some stage in their elections.
On 4 October, voters in Bosnia and Herzegovina became the latest to join the biometric voting club, the same day Brazil, a pioneer of the technology that now boasts 89 percent biometric enrollment, went to the polls. Despite some technical hiccups, election observers say voting was orderly in both countries. Yet as more countries adopt biometric technologies, experts point to significant drawbacks, including high costs, opaque processes and, in the worst case, fallible technology locking people out of the electoral system.
Bosnia’s biometric voting growing pains
Electoral fraud has long plagued Bosnia, says Hasan Kamenjaković, spokesperson for the Bosnian election-monitoring group Pod Lupom, with people voting multiple times, on behalf of others, or on behalf of the dead, often abetted by partisan polling officers. An out-of-date electoral roll packed with people who have died or emigrated made matters worse, says Tana de Zulueta, head of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s (OSCE) election observation mission in Bosnia.
Although Pod Lupom polling found 83.4 percent of the voters it surveyed approved of using biometric technology to tackle fraud, politicians fought its introduction, says Kamenjaković. The country’s High Representative, an official with sweeping powers appointed by the international Peace Implementation Council set up to uphold the 1995 Dayton peace agreement that ended the Bosnian War, had to force through the implementation.
The controversy led to a rushed rollout. OSCE observers reported technical problems with biometric devices at 13 percent of observed polling stations, as well as late openings and procedural slip-ups which they blamed on hasty training of polling staff. Observers also noted problems with ballot secrecy, due to cramped polling stations and poll workers often positioned next to the ballot scanners, and family members joining voters in the booth. But both OSCE and Pod Lupom said election day went relatively smoothly. Bosnia’s ID agency IDDEEA reported a biometric identification success rate “exceeding 97 percent” in preliminary data.
The most significant outcome, says Kamenjaković, was a record-low turnout of 42.02 percent, down from 51.45 percent at the previous election. While hard to verify, he sees it as a clear sign that the technology prevented fraudulent votes, an assessment de Zulueta agrees with. “We now think that this is the real turnout here in Bosnia and Herzegovina,” says Kamenjaković.
Despite those gains, biometric voting technology tackles only a narrow set of problems on the day. Vote buying, disinformation, workplace pressure and misuse of public resources to promote political parties remained rife in the run-up, says Kamenjaković. “We saw so many election irregularities in the pre-election period,” he says. “That’s why we say we are only halfway there.”
In this environment, technology itself can become a source of mistrust without careful handling, says de Zulueta. The election commission leaned heavily on Smartmatic, a British election systems company, to build and run the system, but published neither pre-election test results nor data-handling rules before the vote. “That sort of omission leaves you open to challenges and allegations, and indeed external interference,” says de Zulueta.
Lessons from more experienced countries
Transparency and trust are a core concern around biometric election technology. In Brazil, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) introduced biometrics to tackle similar problems, in particular poll workers voting on behalf of absentee voters. Voters’ fingerprints are checked against rolls using a machine built by TSE before they can vote. If verification fails, poll workers can override the system after a manual identity check, but must scan their own fingerprint, creating a log that can flag irregularities.
However, the TSE has never open-sourced the code behind its election technology, despite saying it would in 2018. It does hold annual hackathons that let security researchers probe the software, but these take place in restrictive, time-limited settings, says Diego Aranha, a security researcher at Aarhus University in Denmark. Despite those limits in both 2012 and 2017, Aranha’s team showed it could reverse a randomization process designed to protect voter anonymity. And crucially, the biometric scanner itself has never been within the scope of testing.
These problems are exacerbated by the fact that Brazil’s voting system has no paper ballots, so “what the software says becomes ground truth,” says Aranha. Because the electoral court writes the software, runs the elections and oversees its own checks, there is “an inherent conflict of interest,” he adds. And opacity can feed disinformation. On election night, a temporary freeze in the publication of results that the TSE attributed to data processing bottlenecks prompted claims of manipulation.
A voter verifies her identity with her fingerprint in Laktasi, Bosnia and Herzogina on 4 October 2026.AFP/Getty Images
Biometrics are also never 100 percent accurate. Bosnia and Brazil have reliable backups for voters who can’t verify their identity, but elsewhere authentication failures have unfairly disenfranchised people. Nigeria used biometric technology in elections ahead of its 2023 elections, when fingerprints collected during registration were used to purge duplicate entries from the electoral roll. Roughly 10 million of 80 million registrations were canceled, says Steve Adeshina, a professor of computer engineering at Nile University of Nigeria, who led the drive as then-director of ICT at the country’s Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).
But in 2021, INEC began using a handheld device that uses fingerprints and facial scans to authenticate voters at polling stations barring voters after three failed attempts. In recent governorship elections in Ekiti and Osun, there were multiple reports of voters being turned away, with domestic observer Yiaga Africa finding instances at 11 percent of polling stations it observed in the Osun state election.
It’s unclear how many were wrongly turned away. But Adeshina notes that faces change with age, and both aging and manual work can alter fingerprints, a concern in a heavily agricultural country. Given Nigeria’s history of widespread voting irregularities, however, he says the risks may be acceptable if the technology removes the possibility of people manipulating the vote. “My attitude to technology is create a monster that you cannot control, so even if somebody puts a gun to your head there’s nothing you can do,” says Adeshina.
However, Nic Cheeseman, a professor of democracy at the University of Birmingham in the UK, says the idea that voting technology removes the human factor from elections is a myth. People still set up and run the systems. And the places most likely to adopt the technology are those with the most disputed elections, he says, usually due to distrust in the electoral commission – the same body that has to operate the technology. “Technology works best where you need it least,” says Cheeseman.
That’s not to say biometrics have no place in elections, says Cheeseman. Using them to clear “ghost voters” off electoral rolls is cost-effective and avoids the logistical challenge of verifying every voter on election day. But using biometrics for voter authentication on election day is not cheap, he adds, and often comes at the expense of more effective investments like nonpartisan election observers and civic education.
That echoes de Zulueta’s concerns about Bosnia’s roughly €38 million system. “It’s going to require levels of attention and institutional structures they simply do not have yet.”
Despite those limits, or perhaps if electoral commissions can take the limits into account, biometric technology still has value to offer, says Kamenjaković, of the Bosnian election-monitoring group Pod Lupom: “At least in this period in the development of the democracy of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is worth it to take the risk, because we really needed a step forward in strengthening that electoral integrity and also democracy.”

candidato.titulo: PowerToys adds smarter mouse controls and more Windows customization
candidato.resumo: Microsoft's latest PowerToys update introduces Mouse Button Lock, which lets you drag and select without holding down a button, and CursorHide, which automatically hides the pointer while typing. The release also adds a quick-access shelf to Command Palette, more keyboard remapping options, and offline voice dictation for ZoomIt screenshots. Read Entire Article

texto_fonte:
Microsoft PowerToys is a set of utilities designed to enhance productivity on Windows. It includes tools like FancyZones for custom window layouts, PowerRename for batch renaming files, Command Palette for quick app launching and file search, and other utilities like Color Picker, File Explorer add-ons, and Mouse Utilities.
Is PowerToys safe to use and does it slow down my PC?
PowerToys is completely safe and it's an official Microsoft open-source project, with frequent updates and visible development. It generally has a light impact on system resources. Users report no noticeable slowdown, and you can disable individual tools if you don't use them.
How do I set up FancyZones for custom window layouts?
To use FancyZones, launch the PowerToys Settings app, go to the FancyZones section, and click "Launch layout editor." You can create a custom layout by splitting your screen into zones, and then assign windows to those zones using Shift + drag. It makes multitasking more efficient, especially on large or ultrawide monitors.
Can I use PowerToys on Windows 11?
Yes, PowerToys is fully compatible with Windows 11. In fact, it takes advantage of some of Windows 11's newer UI features and integrates smoothly into the operating system. Many users treat PowerToys as an optional "advanced mode" layered on top of Windows rather than a replacement for built-in features.
Which PowerToys tools are actually worth using daily?
The most commonly relied-on tools tend to be FancyZones for custom window layouts, PowerRename for batch file renaming, the Keyboard Manager for remapping keys and shortcuts, and the Command Palette (which replaced PowerToys Run) for quickly launching apps, files, and commands. Others are more niche, but useful once you discover a specific need.

What's New
PowerToys 0.102 introduces two new mouse utilities, Mouse Button Lock and CursorHide, a quick-access shelf for Command Palette, and snip dictation in ZoomIt. This release also adds command-line tools for Advanced Paste, Light Switch, Settings, and Peek, brings tap-alone remaps and easier editing to Keyboard Manager, and moves Color Picker and Text Extractor to WinUI 3.
Mouse Button Lock and CursorHide
Holding a mouse button down during a long drag or selection can be tiring. With Mouse Button Lock, press and hold a button for a moment, then let go. Windows keeps treating it as held, so you can continue dragging or selecting until you click any button. This is especially useful for gaming, working in professional applications that require extensive dragging and selection, and improving accessibility for users who find it difficult to hold down a mouse button for extended periods.
CursorHide is the second new mouse utility. It hides the mouse pointer while you type, after a period of inactivity, or both, and shows it again as soon as you move the mouse.
Command Palette gets a quick-access shelf
Compact mode in 0.101 kept Command Palette out of the way until you needed results. Now your favorite commands can be one keystroke away too. Turn on the quick-access shelf in Settings > Appearance > Compact mode to show your pins below the search box while the palette is collapsed. Press Alt+1 through Alt+9 to launch them, or Alt+Shift+number to select one without running it. Drag to reorder, right-click for more actions, and optionally show recent commands and apps next to your pins.
The shelf is just one part of a big Command Palette update:
- Settings search: Fuzzy search finds options, extensions, commands, aliases, and assigned shortcuts, then takes you straight to them.
- Keyboard-first Dock: Press Win+Alt+J to focus the dock and move between its items from the keyboard.
- Copilot key support: Choose Command Palette as the Copilot key app in Windows Settings, and press the key again to toggle the palette.
- Multiple clocks: Pin several dock clocks, each with its own time zone and format.
- Language and links: Pick an app language for Command Palette, and copy links that open a page, run a command, or jump to a specific setting.
- Polish: Sharper app icons, faster grid and gallery browsing, results that keep loading at the end of a list, and clearer nested menus.
Massive thanks to @jiripolasek for the sustained Command Palette work across this release.
ZoomIt adds snip dictation
ZoomIt can now capture what you say along with what you snip. Turn on Snip with dictation in the ZoomIt settings, then press Space while you drag out a snip and describe what you're capturing. ZoomIt transcribes your speech on your device, and a single paste delivers both the screenshot and your text. Dictation uses the microphone selected under Record.
ZoomIt also gets smooth zoom transitions, better audio pacing in recordings, and a fix for silent recordings on multichannel and spatial-audio devices.
New command-line tools
More of PowerToys can now be scripted from the terminal:
- Advanced Paste: Run built-in and custom actions without opening the UI, using files, stdin/stdout, or the clipboard. AI actions use your configured providers and policies.
- Light Switch: Check status, set or toggle the theme, and manage schedules, with JSON output.
- Settings: See which utilities are enabled, and turn them on or off even while PowerToys isn't running.
- Peek: Preview multiple files and folders from the command line.
- PowerDisplay: JSON Lines output makes results and errors easy to consume from scripts.
- On your PATH: FancyZones, Image Resizer, File Locksmith, and PowerDisplay commands now work from any terminal folder.
Keyboard Manager adds tap-alone remaps and easier editing
Keyboard Manager now supports tap-alone remaps. Tap a key by itself to trigger a different action, while the key keeps working normally in shortcuts and mouse combinations. Large remapping lists are easier to manage too, with search, modifier and app filters, and bulk deletion.
The new editor also gets a searchable key picker, so you can select any key, including media keys or keys your keyboard doesn't have, and build a full shortcut with just the mouse. Recording now only listens while the editor is in focus, and Tab moves you out of the recording field. IT admins can also deploy and export remapping profiles with DSC v3.
Other notable changes
- Color Picker and Text Extractor: Both move to WinUI 3, with a new overlay, editor, and magnifier for Color Picker. Your existing shortcuts and settings carry over.
- FancyZones: Scroll the mouse wheel while dragging a window to switch layouts, with an optional indicator showing the selected layout's name.
- Peek: Added read-only SQLite previews, file and subfolder counts with scanning progress for folders, a plain-text fallback, and Alt+Left/Alt+Right navigation between files.
- Screen Ruler: Measure in device-independent pixels to account for each monitor's scaling, with improved edge detection.
- Environment Variables: A new Remove duplicates action cleans up PATH while keeping the original order.
- Quick Accent: A searchable character reference in Settings lets you browse language sets and copy characters directly.
- Grab and Move: Exclude specific apps so they keep their normal modifier-key behavior.
- Shortcut Guide: Added shortcuts for Claude Desktop and Ableton Live, and made indexing more resilient to malformed manifests.
- Workspaces: Now asks for confirmation before launching an unverified app configured to run as administrator.
- Awake: Windows can now turn off the display while the PC is locked, without ending your keep-awake session.
- New+: Fixed a File Explorer memory leak and improved long-path handling.
- Settings: Added an interactive animated welcome scene, fixed a memory leak when switching pages, and kept module on/off preferences when a utility fails to load.

3 melhores notebooks para arquitetos e engenheiros em 2026
Por Raphael Giannotti • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
Projetar edifícios, calcular estruturas ou criar maquetes eletrônicas realistas são tarefas que exigem o máximo de poder computacional possível. Softwares como AutoCad, Revit, SketchUp, Lumion e BIM dependem diretamente de uma combinação equilibrada entre processadores de alta frequência, uma boa quantidade de memória RAM e, principalmente, placas de vídeo dedicadas com aceleradores de inteligência artificial e Ray Tracing.
Para quem busca mobilidade sem abrir mão de desempenho profissional, o mercado brasileiro tem excelentes opções de notebook que originalmente miram no público gamer, mas entregam exatamente a ficha técnica necessária para aguentar renderizações pesadas e projetos complexos.
Abaixo, destacamos 3 dos melhores notebooks para arquitetos e engenheiros em 2026.
1. Lenovo Legion 5
O Lenovo Legion 5 é uma das opções mais equilibradas e robustas para quem busca fidelidade de cor e desempenho gráfico de ponta. Seu grande diferencial para arquitetos está na tela PureSight de 16 polegadas com resolução WQXGA (2560x1600), que oferece um espaço de trabalho amplo e precisão de cores essencial para apresentação de projetos visuais e maquetes 3D.
O modelo vem equipado com processador Intel Core i7-14650HX (16 núcleos e 24 threads, 30 MB de cache L3) combinado com a GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060. Esse conjunto garante fluidez na navegação por modelos BIM pesados no Revit ou na renderização em tempo real no Lumion e Enscape, contando ainda com o sistema térmico Coldfront para manter as frequências altas em sessões prolongadas de trabalho. Atente-se à versão de 16 GB de memória RAM DDR5
2. Acer Nitro V 15
Para quem procura o melhor custo-benefício, o Acer Nitro V 15 é uma escolha extremamente popular entre gamers e estudantes. O modelo traz processador Intel Core i7-13620H (10 núcleos e 16 threads, 24 MB de cache L3) acompanhado da GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060, entregando o poder de aceleração por hardware necessário para cálculos estruturais pesados e simulações.
O notebook conta com 16 GB de memória RAM DDR5 e armazenamento em SSD NVMe de 512 GB, com slots adicionais de expansão que permitem realizar futuros upgrades de memória e armazenamento conforme a demanda dos projetos aumenta. Sua tela de 15,6 polegadas Full HD com painel IPS e taxa de 165 Hz garante conforto visual para longas jornadas de modelagem 2D e 3D.
3. MSI Cyborg 15
O MSI Cyborg 15 é uma excelente opção para engenheiros e arquitetos que precisam se deslocar constantemente entre o escritório e os canteiros de obra. Com um visual moderno e construção leve, o notebook combina portabilidade com a potência bruta do processador Intel Core i7-13700H para lidar com multitarefas exigentes sem engasgos.

Ambient radiation used to power battery-free temperature sensor
Researchers at the University of Arkansas and the University of Michigan have reported the creation of a graphene-based energy harvester that uses ambient radiation to run ultralow-power temperature sensors. This is the second sensor created by the team whose overall goal is development of autonomous sensor systems that draw power from multiple sources in the environment—solar, thermal, acoustic, kinetic, nonlinear and ambient radiation. The findings are published in the Journal of Vacuum Science & Technology B.
The team previously reported successful development of graphene-based solar cells that can be used to power temperature sensors.
The team has three requirements for these sensors: they must use locally harvested energy, they must have a long unattended service life (potentially decades) and they must be able to operate at nanowatt-scale power. All three requirements have been met in the latest sensor utilizing ambient radiation.
MD Rezaul Kabir, a Ph.D. candidate in the Materials Science and Engineering Program at the U of A, was first author on the paper, but graphene energy harvesters are the invention of U of A physics professor Paul Thibado, who began studying graphene's unique properties more than a decade ago and is the corresponding author.
Harnessing ambient radiation
Thibado noted that ambient radiation is everywhere in modern life, especially radiating from the electrical wiring of our homes (though the wires running through the walls could be better arranged to take advantage of this waste radiation). The temperature sensor systems created by Thibado's group focused on the standard 60 hertz electrical frequency commonly used in the U.S. The sensor uses a graphene inductor to harvest energy from the magnetic fields created by these power lines. The inductor's signal feeds into a custom circuit that converts the AC signal to DC, which charges the capacitors in the sensor.
"The inductor adds charge to these capacitors at a slow rate," Thibado explained, "but it's faster than the rate the sensor uses up the charges from the capacitors. So even if the power went out, it can still pull a charge from the capacitors. The way ours are set up, it can easily last 24 hours—probably a week even."
While Thibado's research group is working with temperature sensors as a proof of concept, Thibado imagines a wide range of uses for long-lasting, low-power sensors, such as tracking products, atmospheric monitoring, logistical fleet management, soil and wearable fitness monitoring, and medical tracking, to name just a few niches where he sees commercial opportunities.
Because the sensors don't require batteries, you can "set it and forget it," as Thibado explains, reducing the cost, effort and waste associated with replacing old batteries.
The end goal is development of multimodal (utilizing more than one of the above power sources) sensors utilizing the energy harvesting capability of graphene that can last decades and help realize the internet of things, in which smart technology is literally woven into the fabric of daily life. So a sensor may harvest energy from ambient radiation and kinetic movement, providing a backup power source in the event there is an interruption in one (such as a power outage).

Samsung prepara Beta da One UI 9.5 para antes do que você imagina
Por André Lourenti Magalhães • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
Uma mudança simples no aplicativo Samsung Members alimentou esperanças sobre a possível chegada do Beta da One UI 9.5. O app, usado para entrar no programa de testes da empresa, mudou um banner para convidar pessoas a uma nova versão experimental da interface.
O ajuste é pequeno, não muda o texto e foca na parte visual, mas pode ser um sinal de novo Beta a caminho. A empresa já distribui a versão estável da One UI 9.0 para diversos celulares e tablets desde setembro, então faz sentido pensar nos próximos passos.
Os primeiros testes internos da One UI 9.5 começaram em agosto, de acordo com vazamentos, mas não há indícios de lançamento de versões ao público. Vale reforçar que a variante “.5” não muda a versão do Android usada como base, mas traz uma série de novos recursos para acompanhar a chegada da nova linha Galaxy S.
Para efeito de comparação, a One UI 8.5 ganhou Beta público em dezembro de 2025 e foi lançada em fevereiro de 2026.
O que esperar da One UI 9.5?
A atualização deve contar com um pacote robusto de novidades na interface da Samsung. Uma delas é a possibilidade de controlar a tela do celular em notebooks com Windows, similar ao espelhamento da Apple.
A atualização também pode trazer um novo recurso para criar widgets personalizados com a ajuda de IA. Atualmente, apenas a linha Google Pixel tem a função.
